name: Bilal Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say is confidential. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my brother-in-law Farid, he has a small building firm, five of us. We do house extensions and loft conversions, mostly for families who need another bedroom. I carry the blocks and the timber, I cut what Farid marks for me, I fit skirting boards, and I keep the site tidy. At fifty-eight I'm the new boy, which Farid enjoys reminding me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to building?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I had a grocery shop on the high street for twenty-five years. Then the big supermarket opened by the roundabout, and in two years my customers were gone. Farid said, come and work with me, family looks after family. I'd never held a saw, but I'm strong and I'm honest, and he trusts me with the customers' keys.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like working with family, and seeing a family's face when the new room is finished. My son Hamza lays bricks for Farid too, so I see him every day, that's a blessing. What's hard is learning at my age, I make mistakes with the measuring, and the young ones have these phones that do everything. I don't touch those things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you see, it was all noise. People need people to build their homes. I'd say it after Friday prayers to the brothers, and at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means life carries on, and that's what I want. Seven or eight more years with Farid, then rest, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do exactly what I do now. Work hard, save what I can, we have about three months put by. Maybe Farid will teach me to cut a roof properly, which he keeps promising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the young lads say about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One of them, Tyler, talks about it all day, he asks it how to do things instead of asking Farid. I tell him, the man with forty years in the trade is standing right there, ask him. The machine never carried a block.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Samina say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say alhamdulillah, thank God, and put the kettle on. She doesn't like change either. We've lived in the same house for thirty years.

S0.say: I'd say it was all noise, because people need people to build their homes. I'd say it to the brothers after Friday prayers and at the dinner table.
S0.think: Privately it means life carries on, which is what I want. Seven or eight more years with Farid, then rest, God willing.
S0.do: Carries on working hard for Farid's firm and saving what he can on top of about three months put by. Hopes Farid will finally teach him to cut a roof.
S0.quote: The machine never carried a block.
S0.fieldNote: Bilal frames work through family and faith. He respects experience over technology and is quietly proud of being trusted with customers' keys. He lost one business to a big competitor, which shapes how he sees large companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small builders like Farid will be fine, because people want someone they know in their home. The big companies can have their machines. That's what I'd say to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not worried. Farid's customers come from the mosque, from the school gates, from word of mouth. They don't want a robot in their loft, they want Farid and his family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, really. I'd keep working and watch. If I see the machines on our jobs, then I'll think about it. My son Yusuf would probably tell me to learn something on a computer, and I'd say no thank you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit annoyed at all the talk. Not afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lost your shop to a big supermarket. Couldn't that happen to a small builder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could, you're right. People said they'd always want the corner shop, and then they didn't. But a shop is cheap things, a house is your family's home. I hope it's different, I can't be sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Farid brought in a machine to cut timber, would you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Farid asked me, yes, I'd try, for him. But I wouldn't go looking for it. I'm too old to be the first.

S1.say: I'd say small builders like Farid will be fine because people want someone they know in their home. The big companies can keep their machines.
S1.think: Privately I'm not worried, since Farid's customers come through the mosque, the school gates and word of mouth. They want Farid and his family, not a robot in the loft.
S1.do: Keeps working and watches for machines on their jobs before thinking about any change. Turns down his son Yusuf's advice to learn computer skills, though he'd try a machine if Farid asked.
S1.feel: Calm, a little annoyed by the talk, not afraid.
S1.quote: People said they'd always want the corner shop, and then they didn't.
S1.fieldNote: His confidence rests on trust and word of mouth in his community. When asked about his shop, he admitted the parallel honestly before falling back on hope. He'd only change if family asked him to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's in God's hands, and we look after our own. The government will want to hand out money, but I'd rather work for less than take it. I'd say that at the mosque, and some would agree and some wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it frightens me more than I'd say. If robots can build an extension for half the price, Farid's customers will go, like mine did. I'd be sixty, with three months saved and no skill but what Farid taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for Farid as long as there is work, for less pay if that helps him. We'd cut back, Samina and I, no trip to see her family abroad, no new car. And I'd go to my sons, Yusuf has a good job, he would help, that's what family is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid, but I'd pray and keep busy. Worry doesn't build anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd rather work for less than take government money. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father told me a man who works keeps his head up. Handouts make you lazy and they make you wait for others. Family is different, family gives and takes back over years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hamza, who lays bricks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hardest part. He's thirty-two, he has two small children. I'd tell him to go and see Yusuf about something in an office, and maybe Yusuf would say the office is going too. I don't know.

S2.say: I'd say it's in God's hands and we look after our own. I'd rather work for less than take government money, which some at the mosque would agree with and some wouldn't.
S2.think: Privately it frightens me more than I'd admit, because robots building at half price would take Farid's customers like the supermarket took mine. I'd be sixty with three months saved.
S2.do: Keeps working for Farid as long as there's work, even for less pay. Cuts back with Samina, cancelling the trip abroad and any new car, and turns to his son Yusuf for support.
S2.feel: Afraid, but steadied by prayer and staying busy.
S2.quote: My father told me a man who works keeps his head up.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture breaks his public confidence; privately he sees his shop's story repeating. Family and faith keep him short of alarm. His real worry is his younger son, a bricklayer with small children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for families to prepare. Save, help each other, don't run up debts. That's what I'd tell people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years makes it lighter. I'd be sixty-three, and I could stop then and live simply with Samina, with help from the boys if we need it. Hamza is still my worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save more, another hundred a month, by cutting the takeaways on the weekend. I'd keep working with Farid and see what comes. And I'd talk to Farid about Hamza, about what he should learn while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for Hamza. For me, I can live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Hamza to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, maybe the robots themselves. Somebody must fix them, somebody must tell them where to put the wall. Farid says the young ones should learn that, and he's usually right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd see what comes. With five years, would you do anything for yourself beyond saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm not going to start a computer course at fifty-eight, I'd embarrass myself. My job is to save and step aside for the young ones.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time for families to prepare: save, help each other and stay out of debt.
S3.think: Privately five years makes it lighter, since at sixty-three I could stop and live simply with Samina, with help from the boys. My son Hamza is still my worry.
S3.do: Saves another hundred a month by cutting weekend takeaways and keeps working with Farid while waiting to see what comes. Talks to Farid about what Hamza should learn while there's time.
S3.feel: Uneasy, mainly for Hamza; for himself he can live with it.
S3.quote: Somebody must fix them, somebody must tell them where to put the wall.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him picture stepping aside rather than being pushed. He firmly rules out retraining himself and puts his hope in his son learning the robots. Family remains his whole plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty. Young people should learn a trade now, and families should plan. That's all I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'll be sixty-eight, sitting in the garden, God willing, with grandchildren running about. It doesn't touch me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, save a little, and work with Farid until I'm sixty-five or so. I'd tell my grandchildren, when they're older, to learn something with their hands and their heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly at peace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your grandchildren learn from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To work, to be honest, to keep your word. Those don't change, robot or no robot. I'd teach them to put up a shelf too, so they're not helpless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said worry doesn't build anything. Is there any worry left in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small ones. Whether Hamza made the right choice in those ten years. But that's every father's worry, robots or not.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so young people should learn a trade now and families should plan. That's all I'd say.
S4.think: Privately it hardly touches me, since I will be sixty-eight and sitting in the garden with grandchildren running about, God willing. It does not touch me much.
S4.do: Carries on as he is, saving a little and working with Farid until about sixty-five. Plans to teach his grandchildren to work with their hands and heads.
S4.quote: To work, to be honest, to keep your word. Those don't change, robot or no robot.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he'll retire before the change, so his mood settles fully. He wants to pass on values and simple skills. His remaining worry about Hamza is one he sees as ordinary fatherhood.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The quick one, by 2028. Farid's business would go like my shop did. What would help is keeping the small firms alive, not with handouts but with fair rules, so the big companies with robots can't undercut a family business to nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about trust. When a family lets Farid into their home, they give him their keys. Will they give their keys to a robot from a company in another country? I don't think so, but I'm an old man.

headlineQuote: Will they give their keys to a robot from a company in another country?
portrait: Bilal is a fifty-eight-year-old former grocer who lost his shop to a supermarket and now works as the new boy in his brother-in-law's small family building firm. He's guided by faith and family, never uses AI, and would rather work for less than take government money. He stays calm through the mild pictures, trusting word of mouth and customers' loyalty. The fast AGI picture frightens him privately because it echoes the loss of his shop, but family keeps him from despair, and with five or ten years his worry moves to his son Hamza.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because Farid's firm would be undercut the way his shop was.
whatWouldHelp: Fair rules that keep small family firms alive against big companies with robots, rather than handouts.
